section.title: Introduction and Motivation
section.para: pyReadoutGui is a graphical user interface for controlling experiments that run on FRIB/NSCLDAQ. It can be used instead of or along with the ReadoutShell program.
Why a new control GUI? The ReadoutShell has been used for some decades now. Isn't it good enough? I think the answer is yes but:

listitem.para: The ReadoutShell is a large set of Tcl/Tk scripts. There is some concern amongst the DAQ programming group about the long term outlook of the Tcl/Tk scripting language. pyReadoutGui is part of a long term program to replace Tcl/Tk usage in FRIB/NSCLDAQ with Python components using PyQt for the graphical user interface components.

When FRIB/NCLDAQ was initiall written, experimental scientists were beginning a transition from FORTRAN to C/C++ based tools. It was thought that burdening scientists with learning two object oriented programming languages would be too much of a reach. The simple struture and grammar of Tcl/Tk was considered to be much less of a stretch. At that time, as well, Python was in its infancy and the only GUI components availalble were based on pytk, which, an embedding of Tk widgets into Python, so there was not much user interface value added by using Python.
In the decades that ReadoutShell has been in use I hope we've learned some lessons that can be incorporated into pyReadoutGui.

A rethink/rewrite of the controlling GUI allows us to incorporate into the main program capabilities that, previously, required plugins, these include an expanded capability for event logging, the master/slave capability and event builder configuration.

section.para: The remainer of this chapter is divided into two sections. The first of these describes, in some detail, how to run and use pyReadoutGui. The second describes how to extend pyReadoutGui to support experiment specific needs. Finally, see the 3pyreadoutgui and the 1daq pyReadoutGui reference pages for detailed reference information.

section.title: Using pyReadoutGui
section.para:
This section is a user guide for pyReadoutGui. In this section we'll show how to run the program and some assumptions the program makes. Files it creates and can use are also described. Subsections will describe:
The controls and displays that are present on the GUI and how to user them. For users of the ReadoutShell these controls will be fairly familiar.
How to use the file menu to set up logging.
How to manage data sources with the Data Source menu.
How to set up event logging with the Event Loggers so that your event data are saved.
Using the Slave Server menu to set up pyReadoutGui to accept remote controls from a master. Note the master can be either another pyReadoutGui or, since the user level network protocols are the same, a ReadoutShell
Set up any event builders you need.

To start the program, simply execute the $DAQBIN/pyReadoutGui. The program will look for a python script named readoutguinit.py in its working directory. If that script exists, it will load it as amodule. Next it will look for a script named readoutguiconfig.py in its working directory and, after loading that script it will ask the registered deserializers to load the program's configuration from that scrdipt.

In , we will describe how to extend the set of things that are stored to and read from the readoutguiconfig.py configuration file. This allows you to add configuration information for your own custom extensions. Every second, pyReadoutGui will write the readoutguiconfig.py, updating the configuration to capture changes that you have made.

It is important that if you run several instances of pyReadoutGui they run with differing current working directories. Otherwise, each instance will overwrite the configuration of other instances. If you want to use a common set of extensions, you can make a symbolic link from readouguiinit.py to the common initializer, or, extend the import path and import a common set of libraries:
THe example above shows how to extend the valueof PYTHONPATH created by daqsetup.bash to incorporate a module in /my/library If you have several extensions, separate them with colons (:)

section.title: Running pyReadoutGui and controlling runs.
section.para: For the most part the controls should be self explanatory. At the top is a block of controls that allow you to set the title of the next run, the run number of the next run, select that the next run be timed and its duration.

At the lower right of this block of controls, one or two buttons will be displayed depending on the state of the system. When pyReadoutGui first starts, it will display a Start. Clicking that will boot up the configuration the program has read from its configuration file. This will transition the program from the Not Ready state to the Starting state. If everything starts correctly, the system will transition transparently to the Halted state.
Each state will have its own set of buttons:

listitem.para: The program starts in this state and, if something crashes will return to this state. Nothing is running and the only button displayed is Start which transitions to Starting and, if everything starts correctly, transitions to Halted
The system is booted but not taking data. The Begin is displayed. Clicking that button will transition to Active once all data sources have started taking data.

Data taking is ongoing. If the Recording checkbutton is checked, the data taken will be recorded by the event loggers that have been configured. The End will be displayed and, if clicked, will transition back to Halted If all data sources support pausing runs, the Pause button will also be displayed and, if clicked, trnasion to the Paused state.
Data taking is temporarily paused. The End is displayed, if clicked, ends the run and transitions to Halted. The Resume is displayed and clicking it will resume data taking, transitioning to Active

section.para: Below the run controls are a tabbed widget of output windows. A main tab will show common information and emergency messages. Each data source will have its own tab as will each event logger. The event builders share a common tab. If logging is enabled, messages can also be output to the log file.

More about each tab in the sections that describe what can be configured. We will also see in how to add controls to the GUI. These will typically show up at the below the standard set of the standard controls.

section.title: The File menu
section.para: The File menu is mostly intended to configure logging. Logging allows messages to go to file. Note that the logging configuration is not saved.

listitem.para: This menu entry pops up a file browser. You can select an existing file or specify a new file. Once the file is specified, logging is enabled and log output will be appended to that file.
When selected logging is turned off. To re-enable it, simply select the same log file via File→Log....

section.para: The file menu also allows for the execution of arbitrary Python code within the pyReadoutGui program:

listitem.para: The Python script selected from the file selector that is popped up is loaded into pyReadoutGui. Any code at level zero of the file is executed. Note that the module name assigned to this code is a unique value and therefore it's difficult to use the loaded module in any other code. For things you want visibly availalble, use readoutguiinit.py which generates the module readoutguiinit.
Since the modle is given a unique name, it can be loaded over and over again to get the level zero code execute.
Pops up a directory selector. The selected directory is added to the module search path.

section.para: Finally the File→Exit... menu entry prompts for confirmation and, if it's received, exits the program. Note that exited in this way, readoutguiconfig.py is writtne before exiting. Exiting by clicking the window controls does not gaurantee that, which is why that file is written every second.

section.title: The Data Source menu.
section.para: First a bit on data sources; A data source is something that participates in state transitions. When the state is active, it is presumed to contribute data to the experiment. Normally this means responding to the electronics and inserting events, or event fragments into Ringbuffers. The user interface for managing data sources is the Data Source menu. The GUI for data sources is quite a bit friendlier than the data source management tools in ReadoutShell. This section will describe the Data Source menu. The data source configuration is saved to readoutguiconfig.py and restored when the program starts.

In the ReadoutShell, data sources were assigned numbers that looked a lot like, but were not event builder source ids. In pyReadoutGui this is not done. Furthermore, data sources have a much more granular type, which makes it much easier to properly configure them. The data source types that are baked into pyReadoutGui are:

listitem.para: These are data sources based directly on the SBS readout framework.
This is the Readout and hit sorter pair used to readout XIA Pixie16 crates.
This is the readout system for the Mesytec MVLC controller.

This is the readout system for the Wiener/Jtec VMUSB controller. Note that the CCUSB is not supported directly. If you need it you can add a data source for it or use a ReadoutShell as a slave GUI. Use of CAMAC is being phased out of the FRIB/NSCLDAQ system.
This data source is a programmable delay on begin and end run. It is sometimes needed in large systems between other data sources.
Support for enslaving/remote controlling another Readout GUI (either pyReadoutGui or ReadoutShell).

section.para: Extending the set of data source types is fully supported in a way that allows them to be managed via this menu. See for documentation about this.
With this in mind, let's dive in to the Data Source menu.

listitem.para: Adding a new data source is a two port process. First the menu pops up a dialog with a drop down list of data source types known to pyReadoutGui. Once you selectd a data source type from that list and click Save, A configuration dialog for that data source type is displayed. Fill out the form in that dialog and click Save to create the data source.

Supports editing the configuration of an existing data source, unlike ReadoutShell which required you to delete and re-create a data source to modify it, you can modify an existing data source. The menu pops up a list of data sources. Each data source type is displayed and, where appropriate, the host it runs in, the program that generate the data, and the ringbuffer in which those data are written. If you double click a data source, the configuration dialog for that data source type is popped up pre-loaded with the configuration of the data source you double clicked.
Make whatever modifications you need to make, click Save and the data source will be replaced by one with the updated definition.

Pops up a list of data sources. Double clicking on a source provides the complete detailed configuration of that source. Clicking on the trash can icon in a list entry, deletes that source. Click Ok when you are finished deleting data sources.
Pops up a table of data sources. Double clicking a source provides the detailed configuration of that source.

section.title: The Event Loggers menu.
section.para: In the ReadoutShell, there was a main event logger, that supported maintaining a file system with both run and event file views. Later the multilogger package supported additional event loggers that just created a soup of event files for diagnostic purposes in a directory. pyReadoutGui supports an arbitrary number of both types of event loggers. Furthermore, it allows you to distribute the work of event loggers to ther hosts, while all ReadoutShell event loggers ran in the same host as ReadoutShell. Loggers that mimic the function of the ReadoutShell main logger are referred to a Full loggers.
The Event Loggers allows you to manage the event loggers controlled by a an instance of pyReadoutGui. The configuration of event loggers is saved in the readoutguiconfig.py configuration file.
Let's dive into the entries on the Event Loggers menu.

listitem.para: Takes you through the process of creating an event logger. This happens in two steps. The first step prompts for a name for the event logger, and an event logger type. Event loggers must be given unique names. Enter the name of your logger and select the logger type from the pull down. Click the Save to advance to the step of configuring the logger itself.

The dialog that follows is common between the two loggers, the only difference is whether or not the Full logger checkbox is checked. In fact you can change you mind about the type of logger by checking or unchecking that box.

For the most part the contents of that dialog are self-explanatory. A few additions you may not be used to: The Run in host: text entry allows you to distribute event logging into other hosts. The Logging directory means slightly different thing, depending on the logger type. For multiloggers, this is where the soup of event files is stored. For full loggers, this is the top directory in the tree maintained by the logger.
The Number of event sources should be modified for data from event builders to indicate the number of Begin/End run pairs that are expected for that ring. data.
Note that when you create the first event logger, the tabbed output windows get a tab labeled Event Loggers which captures the output from event loggers.
Lets you remove event loggers. This displays a list of loggers. Double clicking a logger pops up a confirmation dialog. If you confirm, the logger you double clicked is deleted.
Provides a list of the event loggers and their main properties. Double clicking any event logger in the list bring up its full definition.

Loggers can be disabled. A disabled logger is defined but does not log data. Clicking this menu item brings up a list of loggers. Each logger has an enabled checkbutton on its line. Click on them to toggle a logger between enabled or disabled. When you are done, click Ok to dismiss the dialog.
